questions.q: What does the profit and loss account of a business show?
options: The list of all customers who bought from the business
Whether the business has made a profit or a loss over a period of time, such as a month or a year
The number of products the business can make in a day
The market share of the business's competitors
questions.explanation: The profit and loss account (or income statement) shows whether the business made a profit or a loss over a period such as a month or a year, helping make informed decisions.
questions.fact: One important record is the profit and loss account (or income statement). It shows whether the business has made a profit or a loss over a period of time, such as a month or a year.

questions.q: What was ABC bakery's total income for the month ended March 2026?
questions.explanation: ABC bakery's income — bread and buns ₹1,20,000, pastries and cookies ₹75,000, cake orders ₹85,000 and delivery charges ₹15,000 — added up to a total income of ₹2,95,000.
questions.fact: Total Income ₹2,95,000.

questions.q: Which was the largest expense in ABC bakery's monthly accounts?
options: Rent
Salaries and wages for staff
Raw materials such as flour and sugar
Advertising and marketing
questions.explanation: Raw materials (flour and sugar) cost ₹1,00,000 — more than rent (₹40,000), salaries (₹30,000) or advertising (₹8,000) — making it the largest expense head.
questions.fact: Raw materials: flour, sugar ₹1,00,000; Rent ₹40,000; Salaries and wages for staff ₹30,000; Advertising and marketing ₹8,000.
questions.hint: Compare each expense head in Fig. 6.11 with the others.

questions.q: For ABC bakery, the rent of ₹40,000 is a variable cost that changes with the number of cakes produced.
questions.explanation: Rent is a fixed cost — it remains constant regardless of production volume or sales levels; variable costs, like ingredients and packaging, change with production.
questions.fact: Paying fixed costs: rent, equipment costs (ovens, mixers, refrigerators), etc.

questions.q: Accounting helps track what the business owns and how much has been borrowed.
questions.explanation: Through accounting records we can track what the business owns and how much it has borrowed, besides making informed decisions and complying with tax laws.
questions.fact: We can track what the business owns and how much has been borrowed.

questions.q: The profit and loss account is also known as the income ___.
questions.explanation: The profit and loss account is also called the income statement; it summarises income, expenses, and the resulting profit or loss over a period of time.
questions.fact: One important record is the profit and loss account (or income statement).
questions.hint: It is another name beginning with 'income'.

questions.q: In ABC bakery's profit and loss account, the tax to be paid for the month was ₹___.
questions.explanation: After a profit before tax of ₹73,000, ABC bakery had to pay ₹13,000 as tax, leaving a profit after tax of ₹60,000.
questions.fact: Tax to be paid – ₹13,000; Profit after tax (PAT) ₹60,000.

questions.q: Arrange the steps of calculating ABC bakery's monthly profit, in the order they appear in its profit and loss account.
orderItems: Arrive at profit before tax of ₹73,000
Arrive at profit after tax of ₹60,000
questions.explanation: The profit calculation starts from total sales, subtracts total expenses to get the profit before tax, then subtracts tax to finally arrive at the profit after tax — exactly as shown in Fig. 6.11.
questions.fact: Total sales ₹2,95,000 – Total expenses ₹2,22,000 = PBT ₹73,000; Tax to be paid – ₹13,000; PAT ₹60,000.

questions.q: Match each finance term used in the chapter with its meaning.

pairs.r: Total money earned from main operations or sale of goods and services
Profit left after paying the tax to the government
Expense that remains constant regardless of production volume
Expense that changes in direct proportion to production
Goods and materials held for production or resale

questions.explanation: Revenue is the total money earned, PAT is profit after tax, fixed costs stay constant, variable costs move with production, and inventory is the stock a business holds.
questions.fact: Revenue is the total money earned...; Fixed cost remains constant regardless of production volume; Variable cost changes in direct proportion to production; Inventory: goods, materials, and assets a business holds.

questions.q: In a bakery, which of the following is a variable cost that changes with the volume of production?
options: Monthly rent of the shop
Cost of ingredients such as flour and sugar
Insurance of the building
Cost of purchasing the oven
questions.explanation: The cost of ingredients rises as more goods are produced and falls when production drops — a classic variable cost; rent, insurance and equipment are fixed costs.
questions.fact: Variable cost: Expenses that change in direct proportion to the volume of goods or services a business produces or sells... covering raw materials, packaging, etc.

questions.q: Today, India is the third-largest startup ecosystem in the world.
questions.explanation: With consistent hard work and perseverance, India has become the third-largest startup ecosystem in the world, powered by its young and talented population.
questions.fact: Today, India is the third-largest startup ecosystem in the world, powered by its young and talented population.

questions.q: A ___ is a startup valued at over 1 billion dollars.
questions.explanation: A unicorn is the term for a startup valued at over 1 billion dollars; India had around 120 of them in 2025.
questions.fact: around 120 unicorns (startups valued at over 1 billion dollars) in 2025.

questions.q: Match each startup-related term with what it refers to.

pairs.r: A young, early-stage company offering an innovative product or service

questions.explanation: A startup is a young early-stage company; e-commerce, fin-tech, health-tech and agri-tech are the exciting fields in which India's startups and unicorns work.
questions.fact: These are working in exciting fields, like e-commerce (online shopping), fin-tech (digital payments), health-tech (online healthcare), and agri-tech (farming technology).

questions.q: Select all correct qualities for which the Chettiar community was known.
options: Strong business ethics and trust-based lending
Excellent accounting and record-keeping skills
Reinvesting profits into trade, temples, education and community welfare
Refusing to trade with anyone outside their own community
questions.explanation: The Chettiars were known for trust-based lending, excellent record-keeping, and reinvesting profits into trade, temples, education and community welfare — they actually traded widely across countries.
questions.fact: They were known for: Strong business ethics and trust-based lending; Excellent accounting and record-keeping skills; Reinvesting profits into trade, temples, education, and community welfare.

questions.q: Around how many unicorns did India have in 2025, according to the chapter?
options: About 120
About 12
About 1,200
About 45
questions.explanation: The startup world is growing fast, with India having around 120 unicorns — startups valued at over 1 billion dollars — in 2025.
questions.fact: The startup world is growing fast, driven by creativity and technological support, with around 120 unicorns (startups valued at over 1 billion dollars) in 2025.

questions.q: Which of these statements about ABC bakery's monthly accounts is INCORRECT?
options: The bakery earned ₹15,000 from delivery charges
The bakery paid ₹10,000 as interest on its loan
The bakery's profit after tax for the month was ₹73,000
The bakery spent ₹8,000 on advertising and marketing
questions.explanation: ₹73,000 was the profit before tax; after paying ₹13,000 as tax, the profit after tax was ₹60,000. The other figures match the profit and loss account.
questions.fact: Profit before tax (PBT) ₹73,000; Tax to be paid – ₹13,000; Profit after tax (PAT) ₹60,000; Delivery charges ₹15,000; Interest on loan ₹10,000; Advertising ₹8,000.
questions.hint: Be careful about which profit figure comes before and after tax.

questions.q: Which of these statements about accounting is INCORRECT?
options: It means keeping track of the money coming in (revenue) and the money going out (expenses)
It enables compliance with the tax laws and regulations of the country
Every entrepreneur needs to understand basic accounting concepts to know how their business is doing
Accounting involves recording only the money going out and completely ignoring the money coming in
questions.explanation: Accounting records both directions of money — revenue coming in and expenses going out — so that the owner knows how the business is performing.
questions.fact: It means keeping track of the money coming in (revenue) and the money going out (expenses), and making sure all records or documents are correct.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): ABC bakery earned a profit after tax of ₹60,000 in the month.
Reason (R): Its total income of ₹2,95,000 exceeded total expenses of ₹2,22,000, giving a profit before tax of ₹73,000, and ₹13,000 went as tax.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.explanation: Both are true, and the arithmetic in R — ₹2,95,000 minus ₹2,22,000 equals ₹73,000, minus ₹13,000 tax — is exactly how the ₹60,000 profit after tax in A is obtained.
questions.fact: Total sales ₹2,95,000 – Total expenses ₹2,22,000 = PBT ₹73,000; Tax – ₹13,000; PAT ₹60,000.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A business is sure to succeed even if one of its functional areas is completely weak.
Reason (R): The four functional areas of a business work together for its success.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.explanation: A is false — the chapter asks why a business can fail even with a great idea if one functional area is weak; R is true, as the areas work together and provide structure and coordination for success.
questions.fact: Every business has key functional areas... that work together for success; a business can fail even with a great idea if one functional area is weak.

questions.q: In 1931, brothers Digambar and Govind Dandekar started their small business of selling ink powder in
options: South Mumbai
North Delhi
Chennai
Glasgow
questions.explanation: The Dandekar brothers started their small business in South Mumbai in 1931, selling ink powder with limited resources.
questions.fact: In 1931, two brothers, Digambar and Govind Dandekar, started a small business in South Mumbai selling ink powder.

questions.q: Why did the Dandekar brothers travel to Glasgow?
options: To open a branch of their ink shop there
To import recycled glass bottles
To study colour chemistry and improve their products
To attend an exhibition of Indian art
questions.explanation: Noticing that artists in India lacked good art materials, the brothers travelled to Glasgow to study colour chemistry, and later set up a laboratory in India to develop art supplies.
questions.fact: They travelled to Glasgow to study colour chemistry and improve their products.

questions.q: Lijjat Papad began exporting its products only after 2023.
questions.explanation: Exports began much earlier — in the 1980s and 90s, when Lijjat also expanded into flour, masalas and soaps, crossing a turnover of ₹100 crore.
questions.fact: In the 1980s and 90s, Lijjat expanded into other products like flour, masalas, and soaps, and exports began too, crossing a turnover of ₹100 crore.

questions.q: Besides India, in which of these countries did the Chettiars historically operate?
options: Japan, China and Korea
Sri Lanka, Burma (now Myanmar) and Malaysia
The USA and Canada
Brazil and Argentina
questions.explanation: The Chettiars were traders, bankers and moneylenders who operated not only across India but also in Sri Lanka, Burma (now Myanmar), Malaysia and other parts of Southeast Asia.
questions.fact: Historically, Chettiars were traders, bankers, and moneylenders, operating not only across India but also in Sri Lanka, Burma (now Myanmar), Malaysia, and other parts of Southeast Asia.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Chettiars often built wealth without formal banks.
Reason (R): They reinvested their profits into trade, temples, education and community welfare.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.explanation: Both are true — the Chettiars built wealth through trade in salt, rice, textiles and finance often without formal banks, and they reinvested profits in community causes — but reinvestment does not explain how they managed without banks.
questions.fact: The Chettiar community built wealth through trade in salt, rice, textiles, and finance, often without formal banks.

questions.q: Select all correct examples of challenges and risks that a bakery may face, as per the chapter.
options: A guaranteed profit every month without any effort
High competition from other bakeries in the locality
Rising cost of raw materials
Changing customer preferences and volatile cash flows
questions.explanation: Challenges and risks include high competition, rising raw material costs, changing customer preferences and volatile cash flows — profits in business are never guaranteed.
questions.fact: These are threats that disrupt operations or cause losses, for example, high competition, rising cost of raw materials, changing customer preferences, volatile cash flows, etc.
